Constellation

The design system behind Atlas — a three-tier token foundation and a reusable component kit, built from scratch and defined first, so eighteen modules feel like one product and design and engineering ship in parallel.

Context

A product too big
for one-off screens.

Atlas is a donor CRM for Catholic dioceses — donors, gifts, campaigns, reports, legal entities, an AI assistant and more, across roughly eighteen modules.

A product this size needs a shared visual language from day one. Without one, every screen becomes a one-off, the product never feels coherent, and nothing ships quickly.

✦
Why build the system first

Infrastructure,
not decoration.

Building the system up front, before the modules, was a deliberate bet that paid for itself on four fronts.

01

Consistency by construction

If every screen pulls from the same tokens and components, it can't drift — coherence is guaranteed, not policed.

02

Speed at scale

Eighteen modules is a lot to design and build. A kit turns “design each screen” into “assemble from parts”.

03

Change once, everywhere

Tokens mean a color, type or spacing decision is made in one place and flows to the whole product.

04

A dark chrome, done right

A navy shell plus light content needs consistent contrast everywhere — only a token system makes that safe.

The first thing I designed wasn't a screen — it was the system.
The Atlas logo · where the system begins

The system was
already in the mark.

Before any token, I looked at the brand already in the product. The Atlas logo is a constellation — separate stars joined by fine gold lines into one shape, anchored by a single gold guiding star on a deep-navy night sky. “Atlas” itself means a guide.

That mark is a near-perfect metaphor for a design system, so I let it seed every foundational decision.

NAME

Constellation

Many small, consistent parts forming one whole — exactly what a system is.

PALETTE

Navy + gold

Night-sky navy becomes the chrome; the guiding star becomes the accent.

METAPHOR

Lines that connect

The gold lines are the tokens — the connective tissue linking every component.

MEANING

A guide

“Atlas” means a guide, so the system guides the team: one clear reference.

Planning · the architecture

Foundation,
then components.

I mapped every surface eighteen modules would demand — buttons, tables, tags, cards, inputs, overlays — so the system covered real needs, not hypotheticals. Components are only as consistent as the tokens beneath them, so the foundation came first.

1 · Foundation

  • Color tokens — three tiers
  • Typography scale
  • Spacing & radius units
  • Elevation & borders

2 · Components

  • Buttons, inputs, chips
  • Tables, cards, KPIs
  • Tags & status
  • Drawers, modals, tabs, toasts
Primitive → semantic → component: components reference only the semantic layer, so one change ripples safely.
Foundation · color

A token system,
not a palette.

Color is three tiers: raw primitives feed semantic tokens, and components only ever reference the semantic layer — change a value once at the top and all eighteen modules update safely.

Every color also has a job: green always means success, amber attention, rose alert — so users learn the language once.

Why it matters for a dark chrome: because surfaces and text are semantic tokens, the navy sidebar and light content keep correct contrast automatically — no eyeballing colors per screen.
Foundation · typography

Two families,
clear jobs.

DM Serif Display for display and big numbers — it makes money read as considered data. DM Sans for everything functional. Then a single scale everyone pulls from.

Decision: one type scale as tokens, so a dense admin table and a spacious dashboard share the same rhythm.
Foundation · spacing & radius

Spacing as
number tokens.

Spacing and radius became number variables on a 4px base. Designers pick a token, not a pixel — and engineers map each token 1:1 to a CSS variable, so the same rhythm holds across every surface.

Components

Learn it once,
everywhere.

With the foundation set, I built the component kit — each one shipping with its states baked in. Learn a table, a tag or a drawer once, and it behaves the same across every module.

Every component ships with its states

Default

The resting state.

Hover / pressed

Consistent feedback.

Disabled

Clearly inert.

Empty

Guidance, not a blank.

Locked / gated

Entity-gated, shown not hidden.

The system in production

The real test:
very different screens.

Whether a system holds shows on screens that share nothing but the kit — a dense 100-row admin hub and a data-heavy report, both built entirely from Constellation.

A role-aware dashboard — KPIs, cards, AI panel.
A custom report — KPIs, chart toggle, filter chips, detail table.
Same tokens, same components, one product — no per-screen drift.
Implementation & collaboration

Only real if engineering
can build with it.

A system is a shared contract. I worked with engineering to map every token to a CSS variable and agreed rules for how components are used, so behaviour stays predictable and teams move in parallel.

Contract

One component, one job

Every edit opens a drawer; every save fires a toast; every “you can't see this” uses the same locked state.
Meaning

Semantic by default

Status always maps to the same color token, so a new module inherits the right meaning for free.
Handoff

Tokens → CSS variables

Every design token maps 1:1 to code, so design and build never re-litigate the basics.
Parallel

Ship at the same time

A shared kit let design and engineering move on different modules without diverging.
Impact

Assemble,
don't redraw.

  • One consistent visual language across all eighteen modules
  • New modules start from a kit instead of a blank canvas
  • A change at the token layer updates the whole product
  • Design and engineering ship in parallel from one shared contract

Decide once, flows to all.
An honest note: these are structural outcomes verifiable in the product (coverage, token tiers, reuse). Time-saved and velocity gains are real in principle but not yet formally measured — the next step is to track design-to-build time per module.
Reflection

What the system taught me.

The hardest — and highest-leverage — work wasn't any single screen; it was deciding the connective tissue up front, so one person could keep eighteen surfaces coherent.

WHAT WORKED

Foundation-first paid off

Defining tokens before components meant every later module started ~80% done.

WHAT I'D CHANGE

Document as I build

Usage docs lagged the kit; writing them alongside would have sped adoption.

UNEXPECTED

The brand led the system

The constellation logo turned out to be the clearest brief the system could have.

WHAT I LEARNED

Systems are contracts

The value is the shared agreement between design and engineering, not the Figma file.
